passage:
First week of April. Shreya heard it in the college canteen: two boys arguing in Assamese about a cricket match. She stopped with her tray in her hands. She hadn't spoken her own language out loud in Bengaluru for four months.
Bihu, mid-April. Her roommate Nazia found her on the hostel terrace at night, playing dhol videos on her phone, eyes wet. "Home's that good?" Shreya laughed. "In my head the lanes are always washed with rain, and Aita's pitha is always hot. Actually, the drain overflowed every year and I fought with my cousins all Bihu."
A week later. Over instant noodles, she taught Nazia three Assamese words, and felt, for an evening, a little less far away.

qa.q: What language were the two boys in the canteen arguing in?
qa.a: Assamese.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling on the hostel terrace during Bihu?
qa.a: Shreya was homesick, aching for home, its festival, language and lanes, while knowing the memory was nicer than the real thing.

qa.q: What did Shreya choose to do a week later, and how did it help?
qa.a: Shreya taught Nazia three Assamese words, bringing a little of home into the present and feeling less far away.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel on finding Shreya on the terrace?
qa.a: Nazia may be touched and a bit worried, and curious about a home that clearly means so much to Shreya.

grounding: A college student far from home aches for her language and festival, and admits home is more perfect in memory.

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage: Rajni, you're leaving for Chennai next week, so let your Vishal Chacha tell you something. I was nineteen when I went there for engineering. Nobody on my floor spoke Bhojpuri. I'd lie awake remembering the ghats at dawn, the bells, the smell of kachori from the lane behind our house, Dev Deepawali with lamps floating on the river. I missed it so much my chest hurt. When I finally came home that December, the lane was muddy, the kachori man had shut shop, and my brothers fought over the one fan. And I thought, the Banaras I missed was partly one I'd built in my head. Still, I missed it. You will too, beta. Let it ache a little. Then call home, and go eat idli.

qa.q: Where did Vishal Chacha go for engineering at nineteen?
qa.a: Chennai.

qa.q: What did Vishal Chacha realise on coming home that December?
qa.a: He felt wistful, realising the Banaras he had missed was partly built in his own head, more perfect than the real, muddy lane.

qa.q: Which part of Vishal Chacha's advice might help Rajni most in the first months, and why?
qa.a: Letting it ache a little, then calling home and trying the local food, lets Rajni feel the longing without getting stuck in it.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel hearing this a week before leaving?
qa.a: Rajni may feel reassured that missing home is normal, and closer to Vishal Chacha for sharing it. 🙂

grounding: An uncle recalls aching at nineteen for his home city's language and festivals, and finding it more perfect in memory.

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage: Navratri had begun in Darshan's town in Gujarat, and he was stuck in Pune with a practical exam on the fifth day and just enough money for mess fees. His mother sent a video: the chowk lit up, the garba circle spinning, his cousins in bright kediyus. Darshan played it three times in the hostel corridor, the only place with signal. He could almost smell the farsan stall. He forgot, for a moment, that last year he'd complained all nine nights about the loudspeakers keeping him awake. His roommate Madhav, from Nagpur, leaned out. "You're humming again." "Am I?" Darshan hadn't heard anyone speak Gujarati in three weeks. He answered his mother with a long voice note, in Gujarati, just to hear himself say the words.

qa.q: Why couldn't Darshan go home for Navratri?
qa.a: He had a practical exam on the fifth day and just enough money for mess fees.

qa.q: What does Darshan forgetting last year's complaints about the loudspeakers suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Darshan is homesick, and longing has polished the memory, making home seem more perfect than it really was.

qa.q: Why was the long Gujarati voice note a good choice for Darshan?
qa.a: Speaking the language to his mother let Darshan feel connected to home even though travelling wasn't possible.

qa.q: How might Darshan's mother feel receiving the long voice note?
qa.a: She would probably feel warmed and a little teary, hearing her son's voice in their own language during the festival.

grounding: A student who cannot afford the trip home for a festival aches for his town and mother tongue, remembering it better than it was.

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage: Makar Sankranti morning, and Himani was kneading dough in the tiny kitchen of her PG in Andheri, trying to shape ghughuti the way her grandmother did in Almora. The pieces came out lumpy. Pallavi, her roommate, peered over her shoulder. "What are these, snakes?" Himani laughed, but her throat was tight. At home the whole lane would be smelling of jaggery now, and children would be calling the crows in Kumaoni, a language she had not spoken aloud since August. She video-called her mother and held up a crooked piece. "Mummy, remember how perfect it was? Everyone together, the sun on the roof." Her mother snorted. "Perfect? You sulked every year because the water was freezing and the power went off." Himani stared at the dough. She did not remember any of that. She only remembered the warmth.

qa.q: Which language had Himani not spoken aloud since August?
qa.a: She had not spoken Kumaoni aloud since August.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling while she shaped the ghughuti, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was aching for home; she laughed at Pallavi's joke but her throat was tight, and her mind kept going to the smell of jaggery in the lane and the children calling the crows.

qa.q: After her mother's reminder, what choice does Himani have about how to hold this memory?
qa.a: She could keep the warmth of the memory while accepting that home was never perfect, and maybe teach Pallavi a few Kumaoni words so the language has a place in her life in Mumbai.

qa.q: How might Himani's mother see the call when her daughter holds up the crooked piece?
qa.a: Her mother probably feels touched that Himani is trying to keep the festival, and her teasing about the freezing water is a loving way of reminding her that home had its hard parts too.

grounding: It shows a college student far from home longing for her mother tongue, her town's lanes and a festival, while remembering home as warmer than it really was.

passage:
"You're watching that video again," Jyoti said, dropping her bag on the hostel bed.
"It's Eid in my town," Rehana said. "Look, that's our lane in Malappuram. That shop sold the best pathiri."
"You say that about every shop."
"Because it's true! And everyone knew everyone. Nobody was ever rude."
Jyoti sat beside her. "Wasn't there an aunty who reported every boy you talked to?"
Rehana laughed. "Okay. Aunty Kunjumol. She was terrible."
"So not everyone was lovely."
"In my head, they are." Rehana paused the video and hugged her knees. "Here in Kolkata I think in Malayalam and speak in Hindi and English all day. Sometimes I forget a word and feel scared."
"Which word?"
"The one for the smell of rain on hot ground. It's on my tongue."
Jyoti nudged her. "Call your Umma. Ask her."
Rehana was already dialling.

qa.q: What did the shop in Rehana's lane sell, according to her?
qa.a: That shop sold the best pathiri.

qa.q: Why does Rehana feel scared when she forgets a word?
qa.a: Losing a word of Malayalam makes her feel she is losing her link to home, since in Kolkata she thinks in Malayalam but speaks Hindi and English all day.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene helps Rehana with her longing?
qa.a: When Jyoti suggests calling her Umma, Rehana turns the ache into action by dialling at once, which lets her use her language with someone from home.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Rehana's picture of home?
qa.a: Jyoti gently notices that Rehana is polishing the memory, reminding her of the nosy aunty, but Jyoti still takes the longing seriously and helps her reach home through a call.

grounding: It shows a student in another city aching for her mother tongue, her town's lanes and Eid, and remembering home as kinder than it was.
